newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries cling to gains in London, mood bullish.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries cling to gains in London, mood bullish.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries remained in a bullish frame of mind below the psychological 6.50 percent yield on Thursday, but no new gains were registered in London, traders said.
An active morning session saw robust demand, especially in the five-year sector, and economists said data due later would not disturb the market's constructive tone.
"It seems reasonable that there will be plain sailing for a while because we haven't got any (significant) data for about two weeks," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
"We could move down towards 6.25 percent yield in the long-bond but I don't think we will go below there," he added.
Charles Quigley, vice-president at Chase in London, said bulls in T-bond futures had 116-00 in their sight. The September contract stood at 114-23 at 1000 GMT, up 1/32.
The 30-year bond was quoted at 101-27, yielding 6.48 percent, unchanged from Tokyo and just lower from 101-29 in New York.
Traders said a breach of 6.50 percent yield in New York on Thursday following milder-than-expected consumer inflation figures, would tempt new buyers in Treasuries.
"Breaking 6.50, and 8,000 number on Dow Jones seems to have ushered in thoughts of a new era, a brave new world that will provide us with ever rising markets," said Quigley.
Economists also expected Treasuries to remain in good shape until conclusive evidence of an overheating economy was received.
Thursday's data includes June housing starts at 1230 GMT, Philadelphia Fed survey of business outlook for July at 1400 GMT, and weekly jobless claims at 1230 GMT.
Amstad said the main risk on the horizon was the employment cost index for the second quarter due on July 29, and the employment data on August 1.
The U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on July 22 was unlikely to change the upbeat sentiment in Treasuries, he said.
But the current U.S. policy stance would generate above trend growth which would eventually cause inflationary pressures.

"We'll see stronger data and rates will go to seven percent later in the year, but we don't think the Fed will tighten in August and it's not clear it will tighten in September, so we may have to wait until November, December," said Amstad.
He added that the two-year note was expensive at 5.86 percent yield compared to the Fed fund rate of 5.50 percent and the long end of the marker was a better bet.
